oilahuasca_model_reference.label: community model — 69ron / Herbpedia (herbpedia.wikidot.com) oilahuasca corpus, plus the herbs.maxforum.org and DMT-Nexus threads. ANECDOTAL AND NOT PEER-REVIEWED. Recorded here verbatim-in-substance because it is the model the per-plant `enzymatic.oilahuasca_model.roles` field indexes against, and because withholding it while labelling plants by its categories would make those labels unreadable. Source copies: scratchpad/herbpedia/oilahuasca-theory.html, oilahuasca-activation.html, oilahuasca-activators.html, allylbenzenes.html.
what_is_established: Allylbenzene-bearing herbs (nutmeg above all) can produce psychoactive effects. Well documented, including in the clinical-toxicology literature as nutmeg intoxication.

Several allylbenzenes form alkaloid metabolites in animals: tertiary aminopropiophenones (Mannich bases) of three subtypes — dimethylamine, piperidine and pyrrolidine. Oswald & Peele, Metabolism of naturally occurring propenylbenzene derivatives (I-III), 1970s.
They do NOT form amphetamines in vivo. Herbpedia states this explicitly; the dataset's `shulgin_essential_amphetamine_link` entries are therefore flagged hypothetical on every record.
Allylbenzene 1'-hydroxylation by human CYP3A4 and CYP1A2 is documented (Yun et al., Toxicol Lett 137:143, 2003, PMID 12523956, for myristicin).

1'-Hydroxyestragole is glucuronidated by UGT2B7 and UGT1A9 (Iyer et al., PMID 12657745) and sulfated by SULT1A1 — this is the genotoxic-activation pathway in the EFSA/NTP risk assessments, which is the same chemistry the community model is trying to steer.
what_is_not_established: That the aminopropiophenone metabolites are psychedelic in humans. Not demonstrated.

That the enzyme-manipulation sequence below causes activation. The entire activator corpus is self-report from a forum population, with no controls, no assay of the claimed metabolites in the users, and an admitted high non-responder rate ('countless tests have shown that there are individuals who simply cannot get effects from any allylbenzenes no matter which set of known activators they use').
Stevioside inhibition of UGT2B7 in humans — described by Herbpedia itself as 'theorized' / 'potentially'.
17beta-HSD2 induction by vitamin A or gallic acid at these doses.
The claimed potency comparisons ('activated elemicin roughly 250% the potency of mescaline') are single-observer reports.

inhibit.CYP2D6: treated as the single most detrimental enzyme — said to O-demethylate and O-demethylenate allylbenzenes
inhibit.CYP1A2: inhibit; the model blames CYP1A2 for the inert 'melatonin effect' seen with elemicin
inhibit.CYP2C9: inhibit per the later (post-2016) revision; the older Oswald-derived Sequence A had said induce
inhibit.UGT1A9 / UGT2B7: glucuronidate 1'-hydroxy metabolites — a dead end in the model
inhibit.GST (and glutathione depletion): said to destroy the phenyl vinyl ketone intermediate
inhibit.aldehyde dehydrogenase / aldehyde oxidas: inhibit, to stop the aldehyde or ketone being oxidised to an acid or reduced back to the alcohol

induce_or_keep_active.17beta-HSD2 (oxidative, estradiol 17beta: called the single most important enzyme; said to convert the 1'-hydroxy alcohol to the 1'-oxo ketone. If inhibited, the model says activation is impossible.
induce_or_keep_active.CYP2E1: said to 1'-hydroxylate without O-demethylating — the wanted route; glycerol cited as an inducer

amine_donors_for_condensation.piperidine: from black pepper tea and from L-lysine in vivo; the model's preferred amine
amine_donors_for_condensation.dimethylamine: from choline, lecithin, trimethylamine, high-DMA fish — the model says these REDUCE psychedelic effect and should be avoided if that is the aim

pre_use_diet_avoid_list_24h.rationale: 17beta-HSD2 inhibitors are said to block activation for 3-4 h (quercetin) or 4-8 h (grapefruit/naringenin).
17bHSD2_inhibitors: quercetin and quercetin-rich foods or supplements
our_corrections_to_this_list: 'Onions (4.81% quercetin)' and 'Orange (4.58% naringenin)' are Dr Duke's DRY-TISSUE figures, not fresh flesh or juice. Raw red onion is about 39 mg/100 g (~0.04%) per USDA — two orders of magnitude lower. Verified this session.

The list conflicts with our own wiki page The Huasca Phenomenon and Metabolic Redirection, which presents quercetin and apigenin as a protective 'shield' and CYP2E1 as an obstacle. Under this model both are backwards. See NOTES.md conflict 1.

Herbpedia simultaneously lists genistein as a BENEFICIAL supplement while telling users to avoid flavonoid 17beta-HSD2 inhibitors. That is an internal inconsistency in the source, not an error in this dataset.

activator_table.claimed_mechanism: inhibits CYP2D6, CYP2C9, CYP3A4 in humans; leaves CYP2E1 active
activator_table.our_note: berberine's human CYP2D6/3A4 inhibition is real and well documented, and it is itself a significant drug-interaction risk (it raises cyclosporine levels in human studies). That is a genuine hazard quite apart from whether the activation claim holds.

activator_table.claimed_mechanism: unknown; described as a nootropic admixture
activator_table.our_note: HARD STOP ON THIS ONE. beta-Asarone is a genotoxic rodent hepatocarcinogen, banned as a US food additive (21 CFR 189.110) and capped at 1.0 mg/kg in EU alcoholic beverages. The model is recommending repeated dosing of the exact constituent two regulators removed from the food supply. And see NOTES.md conflict 2: ploidy does NOT reliably predict beta-asarone content, so 'Nepalese oil' is an unquantified exposure.

Timing claim is specific: must be taken WITH the allylbenzene, never before, because caffeine briefly inhibits then induces CYP1A2. Caffeine's own CYP1A2 effect in humans is as a substrate and competitive inhibitor; the induction claim at one cup is not established.
Herbpedia concedes this may be competition for UGT2B7 rather than inhibition.

55 mg retinol is roughly 180,000 IU — about 60x the adult RDA and above the 3 mg/day UL. Single large doses are survivable but this is frank hypervitaminosis-A dosing: acute toxicity (headache, raised intracranial pressure, desquamation) and, critically, a TERATOGENIC dose. Absolutely contraindicated in anyone who could be pregnant.

activator_table.agent: black pepper tea, solids filtered out
activator_table.dose_as_published: 5-10 g pepper brewed in 1 cup, filtered
activator_table.claimed_mechanism: supplies piperidine; the model also credits CYP2D6 inhibition
activator_table.our_note: Chemistry check that our own wiki gets wrong: piperine's water solubility is about 9.4 mg per cup, so a FILTERED tea delivers piperidine, not piperine. Pepper tea and pepper powder are pharmacologically different inputs. Herbpedia separately warns piperine inhibits CYP2E1 'which is not good' under its own model, and that pepper sedates at these doses.

activator_table.agent: cinnamon essential oil (Ceylon, explicitly not cassia)
activator_table.dose_as_published: about 200 mg (~7 drops), 1 h before, or in two doses at T-25 h and T-1 h
activator_table.our_note: Deliberate glutathione depletion is the single most dangerous idea in this corpus. Glutathione is what stops the 1'-sulfooxy allylbenzene metabolite forming DNA adducts (EFSA/NTP estragole and methyleugenol assessments) and it is the same reserve that protects the liver from paracetamol. Depleting it while dosing a genotoxic allylbenzene raises adduct formation, and it removes the margin against any concurrent hepatotoxin. Ingesting 200 mg neat cinnamon oil is also a mucosal-burn risk in its own right.

activator_table.dose_as_published: 200 mg (of a 50% extract in the published formula)
activator_table.our_note: high-dose green-tea catechin extracts carry an EFSA-recognised hepatotoxicity signal (>=800 mg/day EGCG). Also note tea is on the model's own avoid list for its flavonols — the source is inconsistent.

activator_table.claimed_mechanism: potent SULT1A1 inhibition; said to induce 17beta-HSD2
activator_table.our_note: kudzu's daidzin is a selective ALDH2 inhibitor (Keung & Vallee, PNAS 1993) — i.e. a disulfiram-like alcohol reaction if alcohol is taken.

activator_table.claimed_mechanism: gallic acid induces 17beta-HSD2 and inhibits GST (but also induces SULT1A1/1A3, so the model pairs it with sulfotransferase inhibitors)

activator_table.our_note: valerian had NO measurable CYP effect in the human probe-drug study (Gurley 2005, PMID 15900287).

activator_table.claimed_mechanism: ground aniseed said to induce CYP2C9; unknown whether the oil carries the active

activator_table.agent: star anise essential oil (Chinese Illicium verum, explicitly not Japanese)
activator_table.our_note: the species warning is correct and important: I. anisatum contains anisatin, a convulsant, and the dried fruits are visually indistinguishable — the basis of the FDA's 2003 star-anise tea advisory (~40 illnesses, ~15 infants).
star fruit is NEPHROTOXIC (caramboxin plus high oxalate) and causes fatal neurotoxicity in chronic kidney disease. A bad choice of CYP3A4 inhibitor.

activator_table.claimed_mechanism: helps nutmeg; said to delay or weaken elemicin in others

activator_table.our_note: the model elsewhere tells users to AVOID grapefruit (naringenin, 17beta-HSD2) and white grapefruit specifically (CYP2A6). Internally contradictory. Grapefruit's own furanocoumarin CYP3A4 interaction with prescription drugs is major and well documented (Bailey 1991).

published_formulas.name: BBSC single-capsule (2017, the current one)
published_formulas.as_published: One size-000 capsule: berberine HCl 300 mg + steviosides 200 mg + niacinamide 100 mg + 1 drop Nepalese calamus oil + 200 mg elemicin (or an equivalent amount of another allylbenzene). Swallowed with 1 cup of strong coffee, taken at the same time, never before.
published_formulas.stated_caveats: calamus can be omitted but 'results will be much weaker'; caffeine is called essential, otherwise an inert 'melatonin effect'.

published_formulas.name: BBS two-stage (2016)
published_formulas.as_published: Stage 1 at T-4 h: vitamin A 55 mg oral + glycerol 5 ml oral. Stage 2 at T-0: berberine HCl 300 mg + steviosides 100 mg + 200 mg elemicin, with 1 cup of coffee.

published_formulas.name: BP3 three-stage (2013, piperidine-based, superseded)
published_formulas.as_published: Stage 1: Ceylon cinnamon oil 230 mg at T-25 h and 196 mg at T-1 h (glutathione depletion). Stage 2 at T-0:30: black seed oil 540 mg + 50% EGCG 208 mg + kudzu 200 mg + Chinese valerian root oil 61 mg + folic acid 0.8 mg + pomegranate 40% ellagic 201 mg + rooibos 20% gallic 100 mg + nicotinic acid 50 mg. Stage 3 at T-0: 100-350 mg 91% elemicin, swallowed with 1 cup of filtered tea made from 5-10 g ground black pepper (solids discarded).
published_formulas.reported_duration: main effects 8 h, residual to 16 h

published_formulas.name: PEA3 three-stage (2013, phenylethylamine-based, superseded)
published_formulas.as_published: Stages 1-2 as BP3. Stage 3: 100-350 mg 91% elemicin + phenylethylamine HCl 300-700 mg + rutin 200 mg.
published_formulas.reported_duration: main effects 12 h, residual to 48 h

our_safety_assessment_of_the_model: Read as pharmacology rather than as folklore, this corpus is a protocol for maximising the bioactivation of known genotoxic carcinogens. Estragole, methyleugenol, safrole and beta-asarone are each genotoxic rodent carcinogens whose activation runs through 1'-hydroxylation then sulfation; the model's own stated goal is to push metabolism down the 1'-hydroxy branch, block the glucuronidation that would detoxify it, and deplete the glutathione that would trap the reactive species. Every step raises predicted DNA-adduct formation. This is the single most important thing to say about it and the sources do not say it.

Specific high-risk items, in order: deliberate glutathione depletion with cinnamaldehyde; 55 mg retinol (teratogenic, above the UL); repeated beta-asarone dosing; neat essential oils swallowed in capsules (mucosal burns, and clove/parsley-seed/pennyroyal-class hepatotoxicity); star fruit in anyone with reduced renal function; high-dose EGCG extracts; and berberine's and black seed oil's own real CYP2D6/3A4 interactions with any prescription the user is taking.

Nutmeg's own toxicity is the floor on all of this: the deliriant course, tachycardia, 24-48 h duration and documented poisonings are unchanged by any activator, and concentrating the oil concentrates that, not a cleaner effect.

Drug-interaction load: a user following any of these formulas is simultaneously inhibiting CYP2D6, CYP3A4, CYP2C9, UGT and SULT. For anyone on prescription medicine that is a multi-pathway interaction stack, which is the reason this block belongs in the Drug Interaction Awareness library rather than being left implicit.

In jerk it is doubly used: in the marinade and as pimento wood and leaves in the fire, so eugenol arrives both from the rub and from the smoke. In pickling it contributes eugenol's antimicrobial activity alongside the vinegar.

chemotypes.note: There is no benzaldehyde in the intact seed. It is generated when the cell structure is broken and beta-glucosidase/amygdalin hydrolase acts on amygdalin, yielding benzaldehyde AND hydrogen cyanide in a fixed stoichiometry — the aroma and the poison are made in the same reaction. This is the single most important chemical fact about bitter almond.

plants.smell: sweet almond: faint, fatty-sweet. bitter almond / benzaldehyde: the intense 'marzipan, cherry, amaretto' note — one of the most recognisable single-molecule aromas in cooking
plants.taste: sweet almond: mild, sweet, fatty. bitter almond: intensely bitter and almond-aromatic; the bitterness is a warning signal and tracks amygdalin content

culinary.why: Almond is two ingredients. Sweet almond is a fat-and-protein ingredient: 45-60% oil, which is why ground almonds enrich and tenderise baked goods by interfering with gluten, why almond milk is an emulsion rather than a solution, and why marzipan holds together on sugar and almond oil alone. Bitter almond is an aroma ingredient, and its aroma is inseparable from its toxin at the point of production: the same enzymatic hydrolysis that liberates benzaldehyde liberates hydrogen cyanide, which is why the commercial article is 'FFPA' bitter almond oil with the cyanide stripped, and why traditional recipes used bitter almonds in strictly counted small numbers. Most modern 'almond extract' is synthetic or fermentation benzaldehyde, which carries no cyanide at all — a genuine safety improvement.
culinary.solubility: benzaldehyde is sparingly water-soluble, freely soluble in alcohol and fat; the almond oil is the fat itself
culinary.when_to_add: benzaldehyde/extract late (volatile and oxidisable); ground almonds as a structural ingredient from the start
culinary.heat_stability: benzaldehyde oxidises readily to benzoic acid in air and heat, which is why almond extract goes flat; almond flour browns and can go rancid from its unsaturated oil
culinary.antimicrobial_preservative: benzaldehyde and benzoic acid have antimicrobial activity; benzoate preservatives are chemically adjacent
culinary.digestive_tradition: sweet almond oil as a gentle laxative and demulcent in European and Unani practice
pairings: cherry and stone fruit (they share benzaldehyde chemistry)

cautions.toxicity: Bitter almonds and other Rosaceae kernels are a genuine cyanide hazard, and children are the highest-risk group because the dose scales with body weight. EFSA's 2016 CONTAM opinion on cyanogenic glycosides in apricot kernels set an acute reference dose of 20 micrograms of cyanide per kg body weight, derived from a 0.105 mg/kg bw exposure with uncertainty factors of 1.5 (toxicokinetic) and 3.16 (toxicodynamic); EFSA notes this ARfD is 25 times below the lowest reported lethal dose of 0.5-3.5 mg/kg bw. EFSA estimated the maximum apricot-kernel quantity consumable without exceeding the ARfD as 0.06 g for toddlers and 0.37 g for adults — i.e. roughly three small kernels for an adult and about half a small kernel for a toddler, and EFSA corrected its own press release to state that less than half of one LARGE kernel could already exceed the adult ARfD. Bitter almonds are comparable cyanogenic material. Oral exposure is far more dangerous than parenteral because gut bacteria hydrolyse the glycoside. Cyanide poisoning presents with headache, nausea, vomiting, flushing, then dyspnoea, seizures and cardiovascular collapse; treatment is hydroxocobalamin or nitrite/thiosulfate.
cautions.pregnancy: Sweet almond is food. Bitter almond and kernel preparations should be avoided outright.

drug_interactions.mechanism: ascorbate has been reported to increase cyanide release from amygdalin — a documented hazard in the laetrile literature

drug_interactions.mechanism: rhodanese needs sulfur donors to detoxify cyanide

drug_interactions.drug_or_class: no clinically relevant interactions for sweet almond as food

cautions.allergen: Almond is a major regulated tree-nut allergen requiring declaration in the US (FALCPA) and EU (Annex II of Regulation 1169/2011). Reactions can be severe. Highly refined almond oil is usually tolerated but is not guaranteed safe.

culinary.why: The leaf's culinary role is as an aromatic, astringent, mildly numbing wrapper: its phenolics and tannins cut fat and richness, and the peppery pungency frames sweet, sour and salty fillings — miang kham is the clearest demonstration, where the leaf holds every basic taste in one bite. As a post-meal paan it functions as a digestive and breath freshener, which is the same carminative/antimicrobial logic as fennel or cardamom. The crucial distinction for a food dataset: the LEAF used as a culinary wrapper (as in miang kham, or Piper sarmentosum in Vietnamese cooking) is a different exposure from the chewed QUID with areca nut, lime and often tobacco, which is a Group 1 human carcinogen.

cautions.toxicity: This is the central caution. IARC Monograph Volume 85 (2004) classified betel quid WITH tobacco as Group 1, betel quid WITHOUT tobacco as Group 1, and areca nut as Group 1 — carcinogenic to humans. This 2004 evaluation went beyond the 1985 assessment, which had found only betel quid with tobacco carcinogenic; the earlier assumption that added tobacco was the sole carcinogen did not survive study of pure areca-nut chewers in the Indian subcontinent. 'Areca nut' and 'betel quid without tobacco' are also listed under California Proposition 65 as known human carcinogens. The attributable disease burden is oral, pharyngeal and oesophageal cancer, plus oral submucous fibrosis. Note carefully that the carcinogenicity evaluations attach to the QUID and to the ARECA NUT, which is a different plant (Areca catechu, a palm) wrapped in the leaf; the leaf itself has not been evaluated as a Group 1 carcinogen in isolation, but it is the vehicle of the practice, and some cultivars contain safrole. Arecoline from the nut also produces dependence.
cautions.pregnancy: Betel-quid chewing in pregnancy is associated with adverse birth outcomes and should be avoided. Culinary leaf use as a food wrapper is a different exposure.

Piper betle leaf is traded as a food/herbal product; areca-nut products face the restrictions.

Herbpedia notes piperine's water solubility is only about 9.4 mg per cup, so an aqueous infusion extracts little piperine while carrying the piperidine. Recorded as a community claim; the established, peer-reviewed part is piperine's CYP3A4/P-gp/UGT inhibition. plants.smell: fresh, woody-terpenic, warm and faintly citrus-piney from caryophyllene, limonene and the pinenes; freshly cracked is dramatically more aromatic than pre-ground
plants.taste: pungent and hot (piperine at TRPV1), with woody, resinous and faintly sweet notes; white pepper is earthier/fermented, green is brighter

cuisines: universal — arguably the single most widely used spice on earth
culinary.why: Pepper does two separate jobs with two separate chemical fractions, and conflating them is the commonest error in spice cookery. The aroma is a volatile monoterpene/sesquiterpene fraction that flashes off within minutes of grinding and within seconds in a hot pan — which is why pepper is cracked to order and added at the end for aroma. The heat is piperine, non-volatile, fat-soluble, heat-stable, and it survives any cooking — so pepper added early contributes heat without aroma. Piperine at TRPV1 also enhances salivation and perceived savouriness, and piperine's CYP3A4/P-gp/UGT inhibition makes pepper a genuine bioavailability enhancer for other compounds in the same meal: the classic demonstration is the dramatic increase in curcumin absorption when piperine is co-administered. This is why turmeric-and-pepper is not folklore.
culinary.solubility: piperine is fat-soluble and very poorly water-soluble (on the order of 10 mg per cup); the aroma terpenes are fat-soluble and volatile
culinary.when_to_add: crack fresh at the end for aroma; add early or into fat for heat and for the bioavailability effect
culinary.heat_stability: piperine very stable; the aroma fraction very unstable
culinary.antimicrobial_preservative: moderate in vitro antimicrobial activity; historically a meat-preservation and masking spice, and the economic engine of the entire spice trade
culinary.digestive_tradition: stimulates gastric secretion and salivation; a core Ayurvedic digestive (part of trikatu with long pepper and ginger, which is explicitly a bioavailability-enhancing formula)

claims.claim: inhaled black pepper oil reduces cigarette craving

aromatherapy.notes: Black pepper oil is relatively benign dermally at normal dilutions (Tisserand & Young give a comparatively generous maximum) but is a skin irritant at high concentration. Note that aromatherapy black pepper oil contains essentially no piperine, so it does not carry the bioavailability effect.

traditional: trikatu (with long pepper and ginger) as a classical absorption-enhancing formula in Ayurveda
antimalarial and febrifuge in folk use

evidence_based.use: enhancement of oral bioavailability of co-administered compounds (curcumin is the canonical case)
evidence_based.source: Shoba G. et al., 'Influence of piperine on the pharmacokinetics of curcumin in animals and human volunteers', Planta Medica 64 (1998) — reported a large increase in curcumin bioavailability with 20 mg piperine

cautions.toxicity: Very low as a food. Piperine is a genuine pharmacological agent at supplement doses, and piperine-containing supplements (often marketed with turmeric) are the real interaction risk rather than the pepper mill.
cautions.pregnancy: Culinary use fine. High-dose piperine supplements are not recommended; animal data suggest reproductive effects at high doses.

drug_interactions.drug_or_class: CYP3A4 substrates generally (e.g. many statins, calcium-channel blockers, ciclosporin, midazolam, some antiretrovirals)
drug_interactions.mechanism: piperine inhibits CYP3A4 (mixed-type, Ki roughly 36-77 microM in microsomes) — raises plasma levels
drug_interactions.evidence: in_vitro, with human PK support from the curcumin and other enhancement studies

drug_interactions.mechanism: piperine inhibits P-glycoprotein (IC50 15.5 microM for digoxin transport in Caco-2)
piperine has been shown in animal and some human PK work to increase exposure to these
weak in vitro MAO inhibition by piperine; low practical concern at dietary intake

cautions.allergen: rare; occupational asthma in pepper handlers reported

strengthens.why: piperine inhibits intestinal glucuronidation and P-gp, so far more curcumin reaches the circulation

strengthens.what: CYP3A4- and P-gp-dependent drugs and phytochemicals broadly
strengthens.why: mechanism-based inhibition at both the metabolic and the efflux step

strengthens.what: beta-carotene, coenzyme Q10, resveratrol, EGCG absorption (as claimed in supplement literature)

herb_herb.effect: the single best-documented herb-herb potentiation in the dataset
herb_herb.why: piperine raises curcumin bioavailability by blocking its glucuronidation and efflux

herb_herb.effect: additive — long pepper also contains piperine
trikatu; additive digestive and absorption effects

Note for formulators: piperine's documented CYP3A4/P-gp inhibition means piperine-containing supplements carry a real drug-interaction label obligation in several jurisdictions.

oilahuasca_model.label: community model (69ron / Herbpedia), not peer-reviewed
oilahuasca_model.note: Cannabis is not an allylbenzene plant and has no role in the classical 69ron activator model. Herbpedia's oilahuasca pages do not list it among activators. Our own wiki page 'Cannabinoid Oilahuasca' extends the oilahuasca FRAME to cannabinoids (CYP/UGT redirection of THC towards 11-OH-THC) — that is a Van Kush Family extension, not part of the 69ron corpus, and should be labelled as such. Separately, beta-caryophyllene is shared with clove, uziza, black pepper and hops, so cannabis overlaps the activator herbs on terpene chemistry while contributing nothing to allylbenzene amination. One real caution for the model: cannabis flavonoids (quercetin, kaempferol) are 17beta-HSD2 inhibitors in the community model's own logic, which would place cannabis on the 'avoid before allylbenzene activation' list — inferred, not stated by Herbpedia.

plants.smell: Pungent, resinous and herbaceous; chemotype-dependent — mango/hops/earth-musk (myrcene), pine/turpentine (pinenes), citrus-peel (limonene), peppery-woody (caryophyllene), floral-lavender (linalool), fresh pine-citrus-fuel (terpinolene). The characteristic 'skunk/gas' top note is NOT from the terpenes but from sub-ppm volatile sulfur compounds (prenyl thiols), the same molecular class that gives skunk spray and lightstruck beer their smell. Aged or oxidised material smells hay-like as the terpenes evaporate and THC oxidises to CBN.
plants.taste: Resinous, bitter-green, peppery; raw flower is grassy and astringent (chlorophyll, tannins). Hemp seed is mildly nutty with no cannabinoid taste. Decarboxylated flower in fat tastes strongly herbal-bitter, which is why culinary use leans on strongly flavoured vehicles (chocolate, ghee with spices, bhang with cardamom/almond/black pepper).

cuisines: North Indian (bhang, bhang thandai, bhang ki chutney)
dishes: bhang ki chutney (Uttarakhand — toasted hemp seed, not psychoactive)
culinary.why: Two completely separate culinary logics live under one species name. (1) HEMP SEED is a food in its own right: ~25% protein with a complete amino-acid profile including edestin, and an oil whose linoleic:alpha-linolenic ratio sits near 3:1 with ~2% GLA — an unusually favourable n-6:n-3 ratio for a seed oil. It is used cold. (2) THE FLOWER is used as a drug carrier, and the technique is governed by two chemical facts. First, cannabinoids are carboxylic acids in the living plant (THCA, CBDA) and are not CB1-active until decarboxylated — roughly 100-120 C for 30-45 min, which is why traditional preparations either toast the material, simmer it in fat, or (in bhang) grind it with heat and long trituration. Second, cannabinoids are strongly lipophilic (logP ~6-7) and essentially water-insoluble, so the vehicle must be fat or alcohol: ghee, butter, coconut oil, cream in thandai, chocolate in majoun. A water tea of cannabis flower extracts very little cannabinoid, which is why the Jamaican/Indian 'tea' traditions add milk fat. Third, the terpenes are volatile and are the first thing lost: anything above ~70 C for long periods strips myrcene and pinene and flattens the aroma, so long low fat infusions trade flavour for decarboxylation. Black pepper is the classic culinary partner on both flavour and pharmacology grounds — piperine inhibits CYP3A4 and P-gp, and beta-caryophyllene is shared between the two plants.
flavour_compounds: chlorophyll and tannins (bitterness in raw/under-filtered preparations)
culinary.solubility: fat — cannabinoids are highly lipophilic and water-insoluble; terpenes are fat- and ethanol-soluble and volatile. Hemp-seed oil itself is a food oil (see the carrier-oil dataset).
culinary.when_to_add: Decarboxylate first (dry heat), then infuse into fat at low temperature. Add aromatics (cardamom, black pepper, rose) at the END so their volatiles survive. Hemp-seed oil goes in at the end only — never used for frying.
culinary.heat_stability: THCA -> THC on heat (wanted); THC -> CBN on prolonged heat/light/oxygen (unwanted, sedating-tasting, weaker at CB1). Terpenes largely gone above ~70-100 C. Hemp-seed oil has a low smoke point (~160 C) and its ALA oxidises readily — refrigerate, do not cook with it.
culinary.antimicrobial_preservative: Cannabinoids (notably CBG and CBD) and the terpenes show real gram-positive antibacterial activity in vitro, including against MRSA (Appendino et al. 2008). This is not a practical food-preservation role.
culinary.digestive_tradition: Ayurvedic vijaya and Unani preparations use it as a digestive/appetite stimulant and antispasmodic; the appetite effect (CB1 in the hypothalamus and gut) is one of the best-documented pharmacological effects of the plant and is the basis of the licensed dronabinol indication.

claims.claim: Steam-distilled cannabis terpene oil is non-psychoactive (cannabinoids are essentially non-volatile at distillation temperatures and do not carry over in quantity)
Myrcene is sedating / 'couch-lock' and raises blood-brain-barrier permeability
Limonene is mood-elevating and anxiolytic by inhalation
The 'entourage effect' — terpenes materially modulate the cannabinoid experience

aromatherapy.notes: The entourage effect is a plausible and widely repeated hypothesis that is NOT established in humans. Santiago et al. 2019 found no modulation of CB1 signalling by common cannabis terpenes at physiological concentrations; later work (LaVigne et al. 2021) found terpene effects at cannabinoid receptors and at TRP channels in mice but at concentrations above those inhaled. State it as contested. Cannabis terpene oil behaves like any monoterpene-rich oil dermally — dilute; limonene and myrcene oxidise to sensitisers on storage. Tisserand & Young do not give a cannabis-specific dermal maximum.

traditional: Ayurveda (vijaya/bhanga): analgesic, digestive, appetite stimulant, antispasmodic, aphrodisiac; sacramental use in Shaivite practice
Traditional Chinese medicine: ma ren (seed) as a bulk laxative; the flower (ma fen) noted in the Shennong Bencao Jing
19th-century Western medicine: Cannabis indica tincture for migraine, dysmenorrhoea, neuralgia, tetanus and as a sedative (O'Shaughnessy 1839 onward; in the US Pharmacopoeia 1850-1942)
Jamaican and South African folk use: infant/adult teas, tonic, asthma smoke
Indian ascetic (Aghori, Nath, sadhu) ceremonial charas smoking — see our wiki Old World vs New World Magic Herbs

evidence_based.use: Chronic pain (chiefly neuropathic) — modest benefit, numbers-needed-to-treat unimpressive, high dropout for side effects
evidence_based.source: NASEM 2017 'The Health Effects of Cannabis and Cannabinoids' — conclusive/substantial evidence; Cochrane reviews are more cautious

evidence_based.use: Chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (oral THC/dronabinol, nabilone)
evidence_based.source: NASEM 2017 — conclusive evidence; FDA-approved indication for dronabinol and nabilone
NASEM 2017 — substantial evidence for patient-reported spasticity; EMA-authorised in the EU/UK

evidence_based.use: Dravet and Lennox-Gastaut syndromes and tuberous sclerosis complex seizures (purified CBD, Epidiolex)
evidence_based.source: Devinsky et al. NEJM 2017/2018; FDA and EMA approved

evidence_based.use: AIDS/cancer appetite stimulation and weight gain (dronabinol)
Sleep disturbance in chronic pain — short-term improvement
PTSD, depression, anxiety, glaucoma, cancer treatment, epilepsy with whole-plant cannabis
evidence_based.source: NASEM 2017 — insufficient or no evidence; for glaucoma the IOP effect is too short-lived to be useful

cautions.toxicity: No documented human lethal dose from cannabinoid toxicity alone — the LD50 gap is very large and CB1 is sparse in the brainstem cardiorespiratory centres. The real acute harms are: panic and acute anxiety; transient psychotic symptoms at high dose; cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome with chronic heavy use (relieved by hot showers and by capsaicin cream, resolves on cessation); dose-dependent tachycardia and orthostatic hypotension with a measurable rise in acute myocardial infarction risk in the hour after use in susceptible people; impaired driving (roughly doubled crash risk, worst in the first 2-4 h after inhalation). EDIBLES ARE THE MAIN OVERDOSE ROUTE: oral onset is 30-120 min and first-pass metabolism converts THC to 11-hydroxy-THC, which is more potent at CB1 and crosses into the brain readily, so an oral dose feels stronger and lasts 4-8 h or longer than the same inhaled dose. Start at 2.5 mg THC oral and wait two full hours before redosing. Paediatric edible ingestion causes CNS depression and has required intubation — store locked. Dabs and high-potency concentrates (60-90% THC) drive the hyperemesis, dependence and acute psychosis presentations. Smoke exposure causes chronic bronchitis and cough; it has not been convincingly linked to lung cancer, unlike tobacco. Vaping-associated lung injury (EVALI, 2019) was caused by vitamin E acetate as a thickener in illicit THC cartridges, not by cannabinoids.
cautions.pregnancy: AVOID. THC crosses the placenta and concentrates in breast milk (it is lipophilic and has been detected in milk six days after use). Associated with lower birth weight and, less consistently, with neurodevelopmental and attention findings in childhood; the confounding with tobacco is heavy but the professional consensus (ACOG, AAP, Surgeon General 2019 advisory) is to abstain in pregnancy and lactation. Also avoid in adolescence where the association with persistent psychosis and with cognitive effects is strongest.

drug_interactions.mechanism: CBD inhibits CYP2C19, raising N-desmethylclobazam several-fold — sedation
CBD/THC inhibit CYP2C9; documented INR rises and bleeding case reports with cannabis and with CBD
CBD co-administration raises transaminases (not a simple PK interaction) — hepatotoxicity signal

drug_interactions.drug_or_class: Tacrolimus, sirolimus, everolimus and other narrow-index CYP3A4 substrates
drug_interactions.mechanism: CBD/THC inhibit CYP3A4; large tacrolimus level rises reported

drug_interactions.drug_or_class: CNS depressants — alcohol, benzodiazepines, opioids, z-drugs, barbiturates

drug_interactions.mechanism: SMOKED cannabis induces CYP1A2 via combustion PAHs, lowering levels; levels rise on stopping smoking

drug_interactions.drug_or_class: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, clarithromycin, ritonavir, grapefruit) and inducers (rifampicin, carbamazepine, St John's wort)
drug_interactions.mechanism: THC/CBD are 3A4 substrates — inhibitors raise exposure, inducers cut it

drug_interactions.drug_or_class: Piperine (black pepper) and other P-gp/CYP3A4 inhibitors
drug_interactions.mechanism: raised oral cannabinoid bioavailability — the traditional pairing, and a real dosing hazard with edibles
drug_interactions.evidence: in_vitro + analogy from piperine PK studies

drug_interactions.mechanism: cannabinoids inhibit platelet aggregation in vitro; additive bleeding risk on top of the 2C9 interaction

cautions.photosensitivity: None known for the plant or its oil. No furocoumarins.
cautions.allergen: Cannabis pollen and the LTP allergen Can s 3 cause rhinitis, asthma, urticaria and occupational contact dermatitis in growers and trimmers. Clinically important cross-reactivity with tomato, peach, banana, apple, hazelnut and other LTP foods ('cannabis-fruit/vegetable syndrome'). Oxidised limonene and myrcene in aged terpene oil are dermal sensitisers.

strengthens.what: Oral cannabinoid exposure, when taken with piperine (black pepper), long pepper or uziza
strengthens.why: CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibition cuts intestinal and hepatic first-pass loss. The culinary pairing is traditional; the PK magnitude in humans for cannabinoids specifically is not established.

strengthens.what: Oral cannabinoid exposure, when taken with a fatty meal
strengthens.why: Cannabinoids are logP ~6-7 and recruit lymphatic/chylomicron uptake; a high-fat meal raises Cmax and AUC of oral CBD roughly 4-5 fold (Epidiolex food-effect study). This is the single largest and best-documented potentiator of oral cannabis, and the usual cause of an unexpectedly strong edible.

strengthens.what: Oral cannabinoid exposure, when taken with grapefruit or other furanocoumarin citrus
strengthens.why: intestinal CYP3A4 inhibition; same direction as the piperine effect, with better human precedent for 3A4 substrates generally

strengthens.what: Subjective intensity of oral vs inhaled dose
strengthens.why: first-pass hepatic conversion of THC to 11-hydroxy-THC, which is more CB1-potent and more brain-penetrant. Not an 'interaction' but the key dose-translation fact.

strengthens.what: Sedation from alcohol, benzodiazepines, opioids and kava
strengthens.why: additive CNS depression; alcohol also raises peak THC levels when taken before cannabis

strengthens.what: Anti-inflammatory and analgesic effect of beta-caryophyllene-rich herbs (clove, uziza, black pepper, hops, copaiba)
strengthens.why: beta-caryophyllene is a selective CB2 agonist (Gertsch et al. PNAS 2008) acting on the same receptor family from the dietary side

strengthens.what: Endocannabinoid tone, with guineensine-containing peppers (uziza, Piper spp.)
strengthens.why: guineensine inhibits anandamide cellular reuptake, raising endogenous AEA — see our Balm of Gilead and Uziza wiki page

strengthens.what: Tacrolimus, warfarin, clobazam levels (clinically unwanted potentiation)
strengthens.why: CBD-mediated CYP3A4/2C9/2C19 inhibition — the mirror image of the deliberate potentiations above, and the reason this plant is a real interaction risk, not a benign herb

weakens.what: Its own potency, with age, light, heat and oxygen
weakens.why: THC oxidises to CBN (much weaker at CB1) and the terpenes evaporate; the single commonest reason stored material underperforms

weakens.what: THC's subjective intensity and anxiogenicity, with co-administered CBD
weakens.why: Contested. CBD is a negative allosteric modulator of CB1 in vitro and a 2C9/3A4 inhibitor (which should RAISE THC exposure), so the direction depends on dose and route; high-dose oral CBD has been shown to increase plasma THC. Do not rely on CBD to blunt an edible.

weakens.what: Cannabinoid levels, with rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin or St John's wort
weakens.why: CYP3A4 induction (SJW via PXR/hyperforin) accelerates THC/CBD clearance

weakens.what: Clozapine, olanzapine and theophylline levels, when cannabis is SMOKED
weakens.why: combustion PAHs induce CYP1A2 — a smoke effect, not a cannabinoid effect; it reverses on cessation and has caused toxicity when patients stopped smoking
cannabinoids are essentially water-insoluble; a plain water tea of flower extracts almost nothing without fat, alcohol or a surfactant

herb_herb.effect: potentiation of oral dose; also the traditional folk remedy for acute cannabis anxiety (chewed peppercorns)
herb_herb.why: piperine inhibits CYP3A4/P-gp; beta-caryophyllene shared between the two plants is a CB2 agonist. The anxiety-relief folklore is anecdotal only.
herb_herb.evidence: in_vitro for the PK; folklore for the anxiolysis

herb_herb.why: guineensine (AEA reuptake inhibition) plus piperine plus beta-caryophyllene

herb_herb.effect: shared terpene chemistry (myrcene, humulene, caryophyllene) and additive sedation
herb_herb.why: same Cannabaceae family; humulene and myrcene dominate both. Hops also contributes its own GABAergic sedation.

herb_herb.evidence: human_PK by analogy with other 3A4 substrates

herb_herb.why: furanocoumarin mechanism-based inactivation of intestinal CYP3A4
both carry liver signals (kava hepatotoxicity; CBD-valproate transaminase rises) and both depress CNS

herb_herb.effect: traditional sadhu pairing (charas plus a pinch of Datura leaf) — additive tachycardia and anticholinergic delirium risk
herb_herb.why: see our wiki Old World vs New World Magic Herbs. The anticholinergic load adds to cannabis tachycardia and dry mouth; tropane dosing is the dangerous variable.

herb_herb.effect: the commonest real-world combination; raises dependence liability and respiratory harm, and smoking induces CYP1A2

regulatory: UN Single Convention 1961: cannabis and cannabis resin in Schedule I; removed from Schedule IV (the 'no medical value' list) by the CND in December 2020 on WHO recommendation.

US federal: marijuana is Schedule I under the CSA. A rescheduling proceeding to Schedule III (DOJ NPRM, May 2024) was pending as of this dataset's compilation — treat its status as unresolved and re-check before publishing.

US: hemp (Cannabis sativa with <=0.3% delta-9 THC on a dry-weight basis) is not a controlled substance under the 2018 Farm Bill; the FDA has nonetheless stated CBD is not lawful as a food additive or dietary supplement, and has issued warning letters on that basis. Delta-8 THC and other 'hemp-derived' isomers sit in a disputed gap in that statute.
US: Epidiolex (purified CBD) was descheduled in 2020; dronabinol (Marinol/Syndros, synthetic THC) is Schedule II/III; nabilone (Cesamet) is Schedule II.

EU: novel-food authorisation is required for CBD extracts (EFSA/Commission position since 2019); industrial hemp THC field limit raised to 0.3% in 2023. EU Court of Justice (Kanavape, C-663/18, 2020) held that CBD is not a narcotic.

State/national legal cannabis markets (Canada 2018, Germany 2024, Uruguay, Malta, many US states) sit above a prohibitionist treaty floor — jurisdiction decides everything here. Nothing in this record is legal advice.
Religious-exemption route: RFRA/state-RFRA and the Shaivite sacramental-use line are the operator's own ground — see the library's religious and legal exemption material rather than this field.

plants.region: Europe, West Asia, North Africa; Netherlands, Finland, Egypt, Canada

chemotypes.name: caraway seed oil
chemotypes.note: Caraway oil is essentially a two-component oil: (S)-carvone plus limonene. The enantiomer matters — (S)-(+)-carvone is caraway, (R)-(-)-carvone is spearmint. Same molecule, mirror image, completely different smell, which is the standard classroom demonstration that olfactory receptors are chiral.

essential_oil.source: Lawrence composition series; European Pharmacopoeia Carvi aetheroleum

whole_plant.citation: the mechanistic basis of caraway's EMA-recognised antispasmodic use; carvone relaxes intestinal smooth muscle in animal preparations

whole_plant.target: potato tuber sprouting enzymes (an industrial aside)
whole_plant.citation: carvone is a registered potato sprout suppressant in the EU — the clearest practical proof of its biological activity

oilahuasca_model.label: community model (69ron / Herbpedia), not peer-reviewed
oilahuasca_model.note: Not a phenylpropene source. Caraway and dill seed are the carvone spices, which is a different chemical family entirely from the allylbenzene spices.

plants.smell: warm, sweet-pungent, distinctly 'rye bread'; carvone-led with a resinous citrus lift from limonene
plants.taste: sweet-bitter, warm, slightly anisic-minty with a lingering numbing quality

culinary.why: Caraway's partnership with cabbage, rye and fatty pork is not arbitrary. Carvone is strongly antifoaming/carminative and has documented antispasmodic activity on intestinal smooth muscle, so the traditional pairing with the most gas-producing foods in the European diet (brassicas, rye, legumes) is functional rather than decorative — it is the European analogue of Indian cooks putting asafoetida and cumin in dal. Carvone and limonene are also antifungal, which supports caraway's role in bread and in kraut. It is heat-stable enough to be baked into a crust, and its bitterness balances the sweetness of long-braised cabbage and onion.
culinary.solubility: fat- and alcohol-soluble; carvone has slight water solubility, enough for a usable infusion
culinary.when_to_add: whole early in braises, breads and krauts; toasted and ground for blends
culinary.heat_stability: good — survives baking and long braising, which is the practical reason it is the bread-and-cabbage spice
culinary.antimicrobial_preservative: carvone and limonene are antifungal and antibacterial in vitro; carvone's registered use as a potato sprout suppressant demonstrates real biological potency
culinary.digestive_tradition: one of the best-documented European carminatives, used in infant gripe preparations and in the classic fennel-anise-caraway digestive tea

claims.claim: digestive, carminative, antispasmodic by abdominal massage

aromatherapy.notes: Caraway oil is low-risk dermally at normal dilutions in Tisserand & Young, with no phototoxicity (unlike cumin oil).

evidence_based.use: mild spasmodic gastrointestinal complaints, bloating and flatulence
evidence_based.source: EMA HMPC monographs exist for Carvi fructus and Carvi aetheroleum (existence recalled; not re-verified this session)

evidence_based.use: functional dyspepsia (in combination with peppermint oil)
evidence_based.source: caraway-plus-peppermint-oil combination products have positive RCT evidence in functional dyspepsia — one of the better-evidenced herbal GI combinations

cautions.toxicity: Very low as a food. The oil should be dosed as a medicine, not a condiment.
cautions.pregnancy: Culinary use customary. EMA-style guidance does not recommend medicinal use in pregnancy for lack of data.

drug_interactions.mechanism: has been reported to reduce iron absorption

cautions.photosensitivity: none — a useful contrast with cumin oil

strengthens.what: peppermint oil's antispasmodic effect in functional dyspepsia
strengthens.why: complementary smooth-muscle relaxation — the combination is the evidence-based product, not either alone

herb_herb.effect: the best-evidenced herb-herb culinary/medicinal combination in this batch
herb_herb.why: additive antispasmodic action on gut smooth muscle

herb_herb.effect: classic carminative tea triad with anise
shares carvone but the opposite enantiomer plus dill ether — similar function, different smell

regulatory: US: caraway and caraway oil are GRAS (21 CFR 182.10, 182.20).
EU: EMA HMPC monographs for Carvi fructus and Carvi aetheroleum; European Pharmacopoeia monograph for caraway oil.
EU: (S)-carvone is an approved plant-protection active substance as a potato sprout suppressant.

plants.region: Western Ghats of India; Guatemala is now the largest producer; Sri Lanka, Tanzania

chemotypes.name: green cardamom seed oil
chemotypes.note: The terpinyl acetate / cineole ratio defines quality: Indian (Malabar/Mysore) material tends higher in cineole and sharper, Guatemalan higher in terpinyl acetate and sweeter

essential_oil.source: Lawrence composition series; Indian spice-research composition data

whole_plant.citation: in vitro screening; cineole is also a known CYP inducer in some animal models — the direction is not settled
cineole has documented hepatic enzyme-inducing activity in rodents — relevant because induction is the opposite of what most 'potentiator' claims assume
in vitro transport studies; weak evidence

oilahuasca_model.label: community model (69ron / Herbpedia), not peer-reviewed
oilahuasca_model.note: Not a phenylpropene source. Included as a culinary and blend-chemistry plant; note that cineole's enzyme INDUCTION in animals runs counter to naive potentiation assumptions.

plants.smell: bright, camphoraceous-eucalyptus top (cineole) over a sweet, fruity-floral body (terpinyl acetate and linalool); unmistakably cooling
plants.taste: sweet-aromatic with a cooling, slightly soapy-floral and resinous finish; intensely penetrating

culinary.why: Cardamom's volatile profile is unusually balanced between a cooling chemesthetic (1,8-cineole acts at TRPM8-adjacent cooling pathways and is the same molecule as eucalyptus's) and a sweet floral ester, which is why it works in both savoury rice dishes and sweet buns. The cooling note is why it is the classic pairing with coffee: it cuts bitterness and adds aroma without sweetness. The whole pod protects the oil — ground cardamom loses its character within weeks because the terpene top notes are so volatile, which is the practical reason recipes say to crush pods to order. Its antimicrobial and breath-freshening use in India is a direct consequence of the cineole content.
culinary.solubility: fat- and alcohol-soluble; enough extraction into hot aqueous infusions (chai, coffee) to dominate
culinary.when_to_add: crush pods to order; bloom whole in hot fat at the start, or steep in the liquid; ground late in doughs
culinary.heat_stability: the cineole and terpene top notes are volatile and lost on long boiling; terpinyl acetate persists better
culinary.antimicrobial_preservative: cineole-rich oil is antimicrobial in vitro; traditional breath-freshening and oral-hygiene use
culinary.digestive_tradition: a principal carminative in Ayurveda and Unani; chewed after meals

claims.claim: digestive, antispasmodic, carminative by inhalation or abdominal massage

aromatherapy.notes: Cardamom oil is relatively low-risk dermally in Tisserand & Young. Standard cineole caution applies: 1,8-cineole-rich oils should not be applied near the face of infants or young children because of the risk of laryngospasm/apnoea — this is a documented hazard for eucalyptus-type oils.

traditional: cardiac and urinary tonic in Unani

evidence_based.source: cardamom appears in European traditional-use practice; a dedicated EMA monograph was not verified this session
small trials of cardamom powder in hypertension; low quality

cautions.toxicity: Very low as a food. The oil is a cineole-rich oil with the usual cineole cautions.
cautions.pregnancy: Culinary use customary; large medicinal doses not recommended.

drug_interactions.mechanism: in vitro inhibition by extract, but cineole INDUCES some hepatic enzymes in animals — direction uncertain, which is itself the honest answer
additive blood-pressure lowering suggested by small trials

cautions.allergen: uncommon; contact dermatitis to the oil reported

strengthens.what: perceived aroma of coffee and chocolate
strengthens.why: cooling cineole suppresses bitterness perception and adds congruent volatiles

weakens.what: possibly the plasma levels of co-administered drugs, if cineole's animal enzyme induction translates to humans
weakens.why: enzyme induction increases clearance — the opposite of the usual potentiation story

herb_herb.effect: traditional chai/garam masala pairing; piperine would raise exposure to co-ingested constituents

regulatory: US: cardamom and its oil/oleoresin are GRAS (21 CFR 182.10, 182.20).
EU: food spice; 1,8-cineole is a permitted flavouring substance.

plants.smell: hot, sweet, sharply spicy-woody; cinnamaldehyde-forward with a hay-sweet coumarin undertone
plants.taste: pungent, sweet, astringent and hot, with real bite; less delicate than Ceylon

culinary.why: Cassia is the robust cinnamon: high cinnamaldehyde gives it the heat and carrying power to survive baking and long braising, and cinnamaldehyde is a TRPA1 agonist, so part of what we call 'warmth' is literally a chemesthetic irritant response rather than a taste. Cinnamaldehyde is also strongly antimicrobial and antifungal — one of the most active food volatiles tested — which underwrites cinnamon's historic role in preserving and in masking spoilage in meat and wine. It pairs with sugar because its aroma is congruent with caramel and Maillard products, and with apple and stone fruit because those carry complementary sweet-sour esters. Fat and alcohol carry it; aqueous steeping extracts less.
culinary.solubility: cinnamaldehyde is fat- and alcohol-soluble, slightly water-soluble; coumarin is reasonably water-extractable, which matters for cinnamon tea
culinary.when_to_add: sticks early in braises, syrups and mulled drinks; ground late or in doughs
culinary.heat_stability: good; cinnamaldehyde can oxidise to cinnamic acid over time, which dulls the spice
culinary.antimicrobial_preservative: cinnamaldehyde is among the most potent antimicrobial food volatiles in vitro, active against moulds, yeasts and bacteria; a genuine preservative role
culinary.digestive_tradition: warming carminative in TCM (rou gui), Ayurveda and European practice

dye.fibre: wool, silk, cellulose with tannin as its own mordant
dye.notes: Cassia bark is a tannin dye rather than a bright-chromophore dye; used more for tannin pre-mordanting in traditional practice than as a colour in its own right

aromatherapy.notes: Cassia bark oil is one of the most strongly dermally restricted oils in Tisserand & Young — a fraction of a percent maximum — because cinnamaldehyde is a potent skin sensitiser and irritant. Never used neat; diffusion should be moderate because of mucous-membrane irritation.

traditional: warming interior cold, 'kidney yang' tonic (rou gui, TCM)

evidence_based.use: fasting glucose and HbA1c in type 2 diabetes
evidence_based.source: multiple meta-analyses; effects small and heterogeneous, and reviews including Cochrane-type analyses have not supported a reliable clinical benefit

evidence_based.use: EMA: Cinnamomi cortex monograph covers traditional use in mild spasmodic GI complaints and mild diarrhoea
evidence_based.source: EMA HMPC (monograph is for Cinnamomum verum bark; cassia is a different species — see cinnamon_ceylon)

cautions.toxicity: The dominant issue is coumarin, which is hepatotoxic in susceptible individuals. BfR and EFSA set a tolerable daily intake of 0.1 mg coumarin per kg body weight per day; BfR notes that for a 60 kg adult the TDI is reached by about 2 g of cassia cinnamon of average coumarin content per day. Cinnamaldehyde is also a mucosal irritant and a recognised contact sensitiser; 'cinnamon challenge' style ingestion of dry powder has caused aspiration injury.
cautions.pregnancy: Culinary use customary; medicinal and high doses, and the oil, are not recommended (traditional emmenagogue, plus the coumarin load).

drug_interactions.mechanism: frequently flagged, but note coumarin is NOT an anticoagulant — dicoumarol and warfarin are 4-hydroxycoumarin derivatives, and plain coumarin does not antagonise vitamin K. The real concern is additive hepatotoxicity and case reports of altered INR with cinnamon supplements

cautions.photosensitivity: none reported for the bark; cinnamaldehyde is a sensitiser rather than a phototoxin
cautions.allergen: cinnamaldehyde and cinnamyl alcohol are regulated fragrance allergens requiring declaration in EU cosmetics; perioral dermatitis and stomatitis from cinnamon-flavoured gum and toothpaste are well documented

strengthens.what: antimicrobial action of other food volatiles
strengthens.why: cinnamaldehyde is highly active and synergises with eugenol and thymol in vitro

herb_herb.effect: well-documented in vitro antimicrobial synergy (cinnamaldehyde + eugenol)
substitution changes coumarin exposure by roughly an order of magnitude

regulatory: EU: coumarin may not be added as such to food; Regulation (EC) 1334/2008 Annex III Part B sets coumarin maxima in compound foods — reported as 50 mg/kg in traditional and/or seasonal bakery ware labelled as containing cinnamon, 20 mg/kg in breakfast cereals including muesli, 15 mg/kg in other fine bakery ware, and 5 mg/kg in desserts (these figures came from a secondary source this session and should be re-checked against EUR-Lex).

US: 21 CFR 189.130 prohibits coumarin as a food additive (section confirmed this session) — this is why coumarin-containing flavourings such as tonka bean are excluded, while cinnamon as a spice is permitted.
BfR/EFSA: coumarin TDI 0.1 mg/kg body weight per day (verified this session).
EU cosmetics: cinnamal (cinnamaldehyde) and cinnamyl alcohol are listed fragrance allergens requiring label declaration.

culinary.why: Ceylon's lower cinnamaldehyde and higher eugenol/linalool make it an aromatic rather than a hot spice, so it is used where the spice should perfume without biting — milk drinks, delicate rice dishes, slow curries. It is also the cinnamon you want for anything consumed in quantity or daily, because its coumarin content is one to two orders of magnitude lower than cassia's. Its thin, friable quills dissolve into a long simmer rather than staying intact, which is why Mexican cooks can grind canela into a drink while cassia sticks are used whole and removed.

plants.smell: intensely sweet-spicy, phenolic, warm and medicinal, with a woody-peppery caryophyllene base
plants.taste: hot, sweet, bitter, powerfully numbing and astringent; the numbing is a real anaesthetic effect, not an illusion

culinary.why: Clove is the most concentrated common spice — 15-20% essential oil, almost all of it eugenol — which is why it is used in tiny quantities and dominates a blend if mishandled. Eugenol is a phenol, so it is a potent antioxidant and antimicrobial: clove is one of the strongest natural preservatives in the spice cabinet, and that is the real historical reason it sits in pickles, cured hams and preserved fruit. Its affinity for pork and orange is partly chemical congruence with their aromatic esters and partly that eugenol's anaesthetic bite balances fat and sweetness. Studding a ham also exploits eugenol's fat-solubility: it migrates through the fat layer during roasting.
culinary.solubility: eugenol is fat- and alcohol-soluble and sparingly water-soluble (enough for strong infusion in mulled drinks)
culinary.when_to_add: whole early in braises, mulls and pickles; ground sparingly and late
culinary.heat_stability: eugenol is heat-stable; clove survives long cooking better than almost any other aromatic
culinary.antimicrobial_preservative: among the most antimicrobial and antifungal of all spices in vitro, and a strong antioxidant that retards lipid oxidation in fatty foods
culinary.digestive_tradition: carminative and anti-nausea; the classic toothache remedy across Europe, India and China

dye.mordant: iron for grey-browns; alum for tan
dye.notes: Used as a tannin source; not a bright dye

claims.claim: warming analgesic in dilute massage blends

aromatherapy.notes: Tisserand & Young set a low dermal maximum (around 0.5%) for clove bud oil because eugenol is a sensitiser and mucous-membrane irritant, and clove leaf/stem oils lower still. Never use neat on skin or mucosa; eugenol causes tissue necrosis at high local concentration.

evidence_based.use: topical dental analgesia (eugenol-based dental cements and temporary fillings are standard dentistry)
evidence_based.source: dental materials literature; eugenol-zinc oxide cements are established practice

evidence_based.use: premature ejaculation / topical anaesthetic creams (traditional combination products)

cautions.toxicity: Clove oil is one of the most dangerous common household essential oils for children by ingestion. Published paediatric case reports: a 15-month-old developed fulminant hepatic failure after ingesting 10 mL of clove oil, with ALT above 13,000 U/L, and recovered with intravenous N-acetylcysteine; a 3-month-old developed fulminant hepatic failure after less than 8 mL and recovered with N-acetylcysteine. Clinical toxicology references state that 5-10 mL of undiluted clove oil has been associated with coagulopathy and liver damage in children up to about 3 years. The mechanism is eugenol bioactivation by cytochrome P450 to a quinone methide that depletes glutathione — mechanistically parallel to paracetamol hepatotoxicity, which is why N-acetylcysteine is the antidote. Eugenol also causes local tissue necrosis at high concentration (a recognised complication of dental use).
cautions.pregnancy: Culinary use customary. Medicinal doses and the oil not recommended; eugenol crosses membranes readily.

drug_interactions.mechanism: eugenol inhibits platelet aggregation in vitro, and coagulopathy is documented in clove-oil overdose
shared quinone-methide/glutathione mechanism — additive hepatic injury

drug_interactions.drug_or_class: drugs cleared by glucuronidation (e.g. lamotrigine, morphine, lorazepam)
drug_interactions.mechanism: eugenol is heavily glucuronidated and can compete for UGT capacity at high intake

cautions.allergen: eugenol and isoeugenol are EU-declarable fragrance allergens; eugenol contact allergy is common in dental workers and in users of clove-containing products

strengthens.what: antimicrobial action of cinnamaldehyde, thymol and carvacrol
strengthens.why: documented in vitro synergy between eugenol and these phenols/aldehydes

strengthens.what: antioxidant protection of fats in food
strengthens.why: eugenol and gallic acid are radical scavengers

weakens.why: high tannin content chelates non-haem iron

regulatory: US: clove, clove oil and clove oleoresin are GRAS (21 CFR 182.10, 182.20); eugenol is also a permitted flavouring.
EU: eugenol is permitted as a flavouring; eugenol and isoeugenol must be declared as fragrance allergens in cosmetics under the Cosmetics Regulation.
Dental: eugenol-containing dental materials are regulated medical devices/medicinal products depending on jurisdiction.
Veterinary/aquaculture: clove oil (eugenol) is used as a fish anaesthetic, with jurisdiction-specific approvals.

chemotypes.note: Cumin is an ALDEHYDE spice — its character comes from cuminaldehyde and the p-menthadienals, not from a phenylpropene. This is why it smells nothing like the other Apiaceae seeds.

plants.smell: pungent, earthy, warm and distinctly sweaty-animalic (the p-menthadienals are responsible for the body-odour association), with a green-terpene lift
plants.taste: warm, earthy-bitter, slightly pungent; dramatically transformed by toasting

dishes: garam masala, curry powder, panch phoron
culinary.why: Cumin's whole culinary logic is toasting. Raw cumin is harsh and the p-menthadienals read as sweaty; dry-toasting or frying in fat drives Maillard and Strecker reactions and partially oxidises/rearranges those aldehydes, producing nutty-roasted pyrazines and a far rounder aroma — which is why virtually every cuisine that uses cumin heavily toasts or blooms it first. It is also a strong partner for fat and for lamb specifically, because its aldehydes bind to and mask the branched-chain fatty acids responsible for lamb's muttony odour. Its earthy base note is what gives Mexican and Indian food their characteristic depth under the chilli.
culinary.solubility: fat-soluble; toast dry or bloom in hot oil
culinary.when_to_add: toast whole and grind, or bloom whole seeds in hot fat at the start; ground cumin added late tastes raw
culinary.heat_stability: the aldehydes are reactive and transform (desirably) with heat; over-toasting makes it acrid quickly
culinary.antimicrobial_preservative: cuminaldehyde is antimicrobial and antifungal in vitro; traditional role in preserved meats and pickles
culinary.digestive_tradition: a major Ayurvedic and Middle Eastern carminative; jeera water (cumin infusion) is a standard Indian digestive

aromatherapy.notes: Cumin oil is PHOTOTOXIC and Tisserand & Young set a low dermal maximum on that basis — a notable exception among the seed-spice oils, and the main practical caution for it.

traditional: jeera water for bloating and nausea

evidence_based.source: small trials of cumin oil drops; low quality
small trials of cumin powder/supplement; modest effects

cautions.toxicity: Very low as a food. Note the 2015 international recall episode in which cumin was found adulterated with undeclared peanut/almond protein — a genuine and severe allergen hazard rather than an intrinsic toxicity.
cautions.pregnancy: Culinary use customary; large medicinal doses and the oil not recommended.
cautions.photosensitivity: Cumin ESSENTIAL OIL is phototoxic — this is the one standout caution for cumin and it applies to dermal use of the oil, not to the spice.
cautions.allergen: Apiaceae cross-reactivity; and critically, cumin has a documented history of peanut/almond protein adulteration making labelled 'cumin' a hidden-allergen risk in some supply chains

strengthens.what: perceived richness and the masking of muttony odours in lamb

herb_herb.effect: the single most universal spice pairing on earth; complementary earthy-aldehyde and citrus-linalool profiles
frequently confused with cumin but chemically unrelated — carvone versus cuminaldehyde

EU: food spice; allergen-adulteration controls apply following the 2015 incidents.

culinary.why: Dill weed's actives are extremely volatile monoterpenes, so it must be added at the end or used raw; the seed, dominated by the much less volatile carvone, is the form that survives boiling in a pickle brine. In pickling, carvone and limonene are also antimicrobial and antifungal, which is a real preservative contribution next to the salt and acid. Dill's affinity for fish comes from its terpenes masking trimethylamine and its green notes reading against fatty fish; the same logic puts it with cucumber (which shares C9 green aldehydes) and with soured dairy.

culinary.why: Anethole is the key: it is intensely sweet-smelling (detectable at very low thresholds), fat-soluble, and heat-stable enough to survive sausage curing and long braises — which is why fennel is the pork spice par excellence, where it both perfumes the fat and reads as sweetness without sugar. Anethole is also poorly water-soluble but freely alcohol-soluble, which is the whole mechanism of the louche in pastis and ouzo: dilute the spirit with water and the anethole drops out of solution as an emulsion. In Indian practice the seed is chewed after meals as both carminative and breath freshener.

culinary.why: Tarragon is the backbone of French sauce work because estragole is fat-soluble and survives a warm emulsion, so it perfumes butter and egg-yolk sauces without needing heat, and because its sweet-anisic note bridges vinegar's sharpness and butter's richness. Steeping it in vinegar is the traditional preservation route: the acid holds the colour and the alcohol-like solvency of acetic acid plus the vinegar's water pulls a usable fraction of the aroma out. With chicken, eggs and fish its anise note sits where a sweeter spice would be intrusive.

It is woody and fibrous, so it is pounded into a paste or sliced and infused rather than grated. Its cineole content also means its character survives the long frying of a curry paste better than ginger's citral does, and its antimicrobial activity is part of the traditional rationale for the heavy spice loads in hot-climate preserved dishes.

culinary.why: Garlic flavour is enzymatic: crushing lets alliinase convert alliin to allicin within seconds; finer crushing = more allicin = more bite. Allicin then decomposes to diallyl polysulfides (cooked garlic flavour) and, in oil, ajoene/vinyldithiins. Heat before cutting (whole roasting) kills alliinase -> sweet, mild. Fat carries the sulfides; browning past golden turns bitter. Black garlic is long low-heat Maillard ageing producing S-allylcysteine and sweetness.

culinary.heat_stability: Allicin unstable (hours at room temp; seconds-minutes in heat); alliinase destroyed by microwave/boiling

culinary.why: Ginger is the clearest culinary case of pungency and aroma living in two different fractions with two different behaviours. The aroma (zingiberene, citral) is volatile and lost on long cooking, so fresh ginger is added late for fragrance. The heat is non-volatile gingerol, which on drying and heating dehydrates to the sharper shogaol and eventually to the milder, sweeter zingerone — which is precisely why fresh, dried and long-cooked ginger taste like three different spices, and why gingerbread (dried, baked) is warm rather than biting. Fresh ginger also carries an active protease, zingibain, with two practical consequences: it tenderises meat in a marinade, and it will prevent gelatine from setting and curdle milk unless it is heat-inactivated first. Its antiemetic use is the best-evidenced medicinal claim of any spice in this dataset.

oilahuasca_model.note: Herbpedia 'Oilahuasca Activators' lists kava under 'CYP2E1 Inhibitors to Avoid' — the model holds CYP2E1 activity is needed for allylbenzene 1'-hydroxylation. The human PK fact (Gurley 2005: kava cuts CYP2E1 ~40%) is real; the conclusion that this blocks oilahuasca is the community model. Kava's methylenedioxyphenyl kavalactones are themselves mechanism-based CYP inhibitors (MI complex at 455 nm). The community model's own enzyme map, pre-use diet avoid-list, activator table with doses as published, and the full formulas are recorded at dataset level in meta.oilahuasca_model_reference, together with our hazard assessment of them.

culinary.solubility: fat — kavalactones are lipophilic; water preparations are emulsions. Ethanol/acetone extracts pull a different, flavokavain-richer profile.

culinary.antimicrobial_preservative: Low pH is a genuine preservative: lemon juice is used in canning to bring tomato preparations into a safe acid range, and inhibits enzymatic browning.

culinary.why: Lime acid denatures fish protein in ceviche, which 'cooks' it without heat; it is the acid of choice where a bitter-resinous edge is wanted rather than lemon's sweetness. Distilled lime oil's rearranged terpineol/cineole profile is the cola flavour. Dried Persian limes ferment and oxidise to a musty-sour note that survives long stewing.
culinary.solubility: split — oil in the zest (fat-soluble), acid in the juice (water-soluble)
culinary.when_to_add: Squeeze at the last moment; lime juice turns bitter and dull on standing because limonin oxidises and citral degrades. Zest into fat or sugar.

culinary.antimicrobial_preservative: Low pH preservation; antimicrobial in marinades (but ceviche acid does not reliably kill parasites or Vibrio).

aromatherapy.notes: Expressed lime oil is strongly phototoxic and is restricted by IFRA to 0.70% in leave-on products; distilled lime oil is not phototoxic.

cautions.pregnancy: Culinary fine.
cautions.photosensitivity: Yes — the textbook phytophotodermatitis citrus. Lime juice or peel on skin plus UVA causes bullous dermatitis and long-lasting hyperpigmentation ('margarita burn', 'bartender's dermatitis'). Expressed oil IFRA-limited to 0.70% leave-on.
cautions.allergen: Limonene/citral declarable allergens; furanocoumarin phototoxic reactions are far more common than true allergy.

culinary.why: Historically long pepper, not black pepper, was the prestige pepper: Pliny priced it higher, and it dominates Apicius. It fell out of European use as the black pepper trade scaled. Chemically it delivers more piperine per gram with a sweeter, more aromatic sesquiterpene background, so it reads as 'pepper plus warm spice' in one ingredient. Its slow heat comes from the same TRPV1 agonism but with a different dissolution profile in fat. In Ayurveda its central role is explicitly as a yogavahi — an absorption enhancer put into formulas precisely to increase the uptake of everything else, which is the traditional articulation of the piperine mechanism.
culinary.solubility: piperine fat-soluble, poorly water-soluble; aroma terpenes fat-soluble
culinary.when_to_add: ground into blends and rubs; infused into fat, honey or spirit; whole spikes in long braises
culinary.heat_stability: piperine stable; aroma fraction volatile
culinary.digestive_tradition: a cornerstone Ayurvedic digestive and absorption enhancer (trikatu = long pepper + black pepper + ginger)

cautions.toxicity: Food spice at culinary doses. Piperlongumine is cytotoxic in vitro and the plant's extracts are more pharmacologically active than black pepper's; concentrated extracts deserve more caution than the spice.
cautions.pregnancy: Avoid medicinal doses; Ayurvedic texts and animal data both counsel caution, and high-dose piperine has reproductive effects in rodents.

culinary.why: Nutmeg's volatiles are lipophilic terpenes and phenylpropenes, so they dissolve into dairy fat and egg yolk and read as 'richness' rather than as a distinct spice note — which is why it is the classic spice for cream sauces, potatoes, cheese and custard. Its terpinen-4-ol and myristicin fraction also mutes the sulfurous and amine notes of brassicas, spinach and offal.
culinary.solubility: fat — the phenylpropenes and monoterpenes are poorly water-soluble; infuse into butter, cream or oil for full expression
culinary.when_to_add: grate fresh at the end or into the fat phase; pre-ground nutmeg loses the monoterpene top notes within weeks
culinary.heat_stability: monoterpenes (sabinene, pinenes) are volatile and lost on long boiling; the heavier phenylpropenes survive baking, so baked goods keep the warm-resinous character while losing the fresh pine note
culinary.antimicrobial_preservative: nutmeg oil is active in vitro against Gram-positive bacteria and food moulds; historically used in sausage curing alongside salt and nitrite
culinary.digestive_tradition: carminative and anti-diarrhoeal in Ayurveda, Unani and European folk practice; the fixed oil and lignans are the usual attribution

claims.claim: warming, stimulating, used for muscular aches in massage dilution
analgesic / anti-inflammatory activity of the oil

aromatherapy.notes: Tisserand & Young set a dermal maximum for nutmeg oil (low single-digit percent) on the basis of the myristicin/safrole content and recommend avoiding it in pregnancy; the East Indian type is the more restricted.

evidence_based.use: no established clinical indication at culinary or supplement doses
evidence_based.source: no EMA monograph for Myristicae semen located

cautions.toxicity: Large single ingestions (on the order of one to several whole nutmegs, i.e. several grams of kernel) cause an unpleasant and sometimes medically significant anticholinergic-like syndrome: tachycardia, flushing, dry mouth, nausea, agitation, confusion, and a prolonged hangover lasting a day or more. Poison-centre case series are numerous and the course is described as distressing rather than desirable. Hepatic injury has been reported in overdose.
cautions.pregnancy: Avoid medicinal or high doses; myristicin and safrole cross the placenta and the oil is traditionally regarded as abortifacient. Culinary pinches are not the concern.

drug_interactions.mechanism: weak MAO inhibition plus unclear central effects
additive anticholinergic-like toxicity at overdose quantities

cautions.allergen: contact dermatitis reported rarely to the oil; not a major food allergen

herb_herb.why: piperine is an established CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitor; nutmeg adds in vitro CYP inhibition

EU: Regulation (EC) 1334/2008 Annex III restricts added safrole and methyleugenol in foods; naturally present amounts in nutmeg used as a spice are handled through the Annex III compound-food limits rather than a ban on the spice.

plants.smell: sweet, warm, root-beer-like — safrole is the defining 'root beer' aroma; soft, balsamic, faintly camphoraceous
plants.taste: sweet-aromatic, slightly numbing; the leaf (file) is mild, green and mucilaginous rather than safrole-flavoured

dishes: historic root beer and sassafras tea (now reformulated or banned)
culinary.why: Two completely different culinary stories live in this plant. The leaf, dried and ground as file powder, is used for its mucilage: added off the heat at the end of a gumbo it thickens by hydrating polysaccharides, and boiling it makes it stringy — this use carries essentially no safrole and remains standard in Louisiana cooking. The root bark is the safrole part, and that is the part removed from the food supply. Modern commercial root beer uses safrole-free sassafras extract or wintergreen/vanilla/anise substitutes. The sweet root-beer smell people associate with sassafras is literally the smell of safrole.
flavour_compounds: leaf: green C6 aldehydes, mucilage (textural rather than aromatic)
culinary.solubility: safrole is fat- and alcohol-soluble, poorly water-soluble; the leaf mucilage is water-hydrating
culinary.when_to_add: file powder is stirred in off the heat at the end of a gumbo, never boiled
culinary.heat_stability: safrole is heat-stable; the leaf mucilage is degraded by boiling (loses thickening, turns ropy)
culinary.antimicrobial_preservative: the oil is antimicrobial and historically insecticidal/pediculicidal
culinary.digestive_tradition: spring tonic, 'blood thinner' and diaphoretic in Appalachian and Native American practice

dye.compound: tannins and flavonoid pigments in bark and root
dye.notes: A minor historic North American bark dye, overshadowed by its aromatic uses

claims.claim: not used — the oil is effectively excluded from aromatherapy practice

aromatherapy.notes: Tisserand & Young list sassafras oil among the oils that should not be used, on safrole content; it is also a controlled precursor in many jurisdictions.

evidence_based.use: no approved therapeutic use; withdrawn from the food supply on carcinogenicity grounds
file powder as a culinary thickener (non-medicinal)

cautions.toxicity: Safrole is a rodent hepatocarcinogen, acting through CYP-mediated 1'-hydroxylation then sulfation to a DNA-reactive ester. Sassafras root-bark tea and sassafras oil are therefore not safe beverages or medicines. Acute safrole overdose causes vomiting, hypotension, hallucination, hepatic injury and has been fatal. The leaf (file) is a separate matter and remains in culinary use.
cautions.pregnancy: Contraindicated in any form other than the leaf as a culinary thickener.

drug_interactions.mechanism: CYP2E1 interplay and additive hepatic stress

strengthens.why: safrole is a mechanism-based CYP inhibitor

regulatory: US: safrole is prohibited as a food additive — 21 CFR 189.180 (section confirmed present in Part 189 Subpart C this session); sassafras oil and safrole-containing sassafras were removed from food and beverage use in 1960, and safrole-free sassafras extract is what commercial root beer now uses.
US: safrole is a DEA List I chemical (controlled precursor), so bulk oil is regulated beyond food law.

EU: safrole may not be added as such to food under Regulation (EC) 1334/2008 Annex III Part A; the earlier Directive 88/388/EEC had set a 1 mg/kg general foodstuff limit. No current Part B maximum for safrole was retrieved this session.
File (ground sassafras leaf) remains in ordinary culinary use.

culinary.why: Roasting creates furfurylthiol and pyrazines by Maillard chemistry from the seed's sugars and sulfur amino acids, which is why toasted sesame oil smells nothing like cold-pressed. Sesamol and gamma-tocopherol make sesame oil unusually oxidation-resistant for a polyunsaturated oil. Ground seed emulsifies into tahini, carrying both fat and protein.

culinary.when_to_add: Toasted sesame oil is a finishing oil, added off the heat; refined light sesame oil can be cooked with. Toast seeds just to fragrance, they burn fast.
culinary.heat_stability: The roast volatiles are destroyed by further high heat — the reason toasted oil is never used for frying. The fixed oil itself is relatively stable thanks to sesamol and tocopherol.
culinary.antimicrobial_preservative: Sesamol is an antioxidant preservative in the oil, extending its shelf life relative to other polyunsaturated oils.
culinary.digestive_tradition: Ayurveda treats til oil as the base vehicle for abhyanga massage and for medicated oils; warming and vata-pacifying.

cautions.allergen: Major allergen. Sesame is a named priority allergen in the EU, and in the US the FASTER Act 2021 made it the ninth labelled major food allergen from 1 January 2023. Anaphylaxis documented; refined oil may still carry protein.
