culinary.why: The 'ma' of málà comes from hydroxy-alpha-sanshool blocking two-pore potassium channels in touch-sensitive and nociceptive fibres, so lips feel vibration. It pairs with chili ('la') because the tingle makes capsaicin heat feel less sharp and more layered. Linalool/limonene give the floral top note that cuts fatty broth.
culinary.solubility: both — sanshools are lipophilic amides and extract into hot oil (hua jiao you); linalool is volatile and fat-soluble
culinary.when_to_add: Toast husks briefly then grind fresh; infuse whole in oil at 120-150 C, or finish with ground powder at the end.
culinary.heat_stability: Sanshools oxidise and isomerise quickly once ground (tingle fades within weeks); hot oil infusion stable for months if kept cool/dark. Over-frying turns them bitter.
culinary.antimicrobial_preservative: Pericarp extracts antibacterial in vitro; traditional preservative role in pickled vegetables.
culinary.digestive_tradition: TCM warming herb: 'warms the middle', stops pain, kills parasites; used for cold abdominal pain and diarrhoea.

cautions.pregnancy: Culinary use fine; TCM lists caution in pregnancy for large doses (traditional only).
cautions.photosensitivity: No (furanocoumarins not significant in pericarp; some Zanthoxylum barks contain them).
cautions.allergen: Rutaceae—possible cross-reactivity with citrus; rare. Historically imported husks carried citrus-canker risk (US import ban 1968-2005 on phytosanitary grounds, not toxicity).

culinary.why: Star anise is the long-cook anise: its anethole is carried on a heavy, resinous base that survives hours of simmering, so unlike aniseed or fennel fronds it is designed into broths and master stocks. In braises it works with glutamate and with Maillard-derived meaty compounds to deepen perceived savouriness — the reason one or two pods transform a beef broth. It also has a genuine synergy with onion/allium and with cassia in the five-spice structure. Used too heavily it dominates and reads medicinal.
culinary.solubility: the anethole is fat- and alcohol-soluble, but enough migrates into a long aqueous braise to flavour it strongly; whole pods in water is the standard technique
culinary.when_to_add: whole, at the start of a braise or broth; remove before it dominates
culinary.heat_stability: very good — the signature long-simmer spice
culinary.antimicrobial_preservative: anethole and the extract have in vitro antibacterial and antifungal activity; traditional role in preserved eggs and master stocks
culinary.digestive_tradition: carminative and stomachic in TCM (ba jiao hui xiang, used to warm the middle and dispel cold)

aromatherapy.notes: Tisserand & Young treat star anise oil similarly to anise oil — restricted dermal maximum, avoid in pregnancy and in children, on anethole/estragole grounds.

traditional: colic remedy in infusion (the practice that caused the poisonings below)

evidence_based.source: pharmaceutical manufacturing literature — this is a chemical-supply fact, not a therapeutic claim for the spice

evidence_based.use: no approved clinical indication for the spice itself

cautions.toxicity: Chinese star anise (I. verum) is regarded by FDA as GRAS. The hazard is adulteration with Japanese star anise (Illicium anisatum), which contains the potent neurotoxic sesquiterpene lactones anisatin and neoanisatin (non-competitive GABA-A antagonists, hence seizures). On 10 September 2003 the FDA advised consumers not to drink star-anise teas after about 40 illnesses including roughly 15 infants, with seizures, vomiting, jitteriness and nystagmus; the agency could not determine whether the implicated material was Japanese, Chinese or mixed, and noted that the dried fruits of the two species cannot be told apart visually. All affected individuals recovered. AHPA later published trade guidance for differentiating the species.
cautions.pregnancy: Culinary use customary; medicinal infusions and the oil are not recommended, and infant use is specifically advised against.

drug_interactions.mechanism: if the material is adulterated with I. anisatum, anisatin is a GABA-A antagonist and proconvulsant — this is an adulteration hazard rather than a true interaction

strengthens.what: savoury perception in long braises (culinary, not pharmacological)
strengthens.why: aroma-taste interaction with glutamate and Maillard products

herb_herb.why: cinnamaldehyde plus anethole plus eugenol cover complementary aroma classes

regulatory: US: Illicium verum is GRAS as a spice; FDA consumer advisory of 10 September 2003 against star-anise teas because of possible Illicium anisatum contamination (confirmed this session).
EU: Illicium anisatum is not permitted in food; species authentication is a recognised control point.
EU: Annex III of Regulation (EC) 1334/2008 estragole limits apply to compound foods.

culinary.why: Basil's actives are among the most fragile in the herb world: linalool is volatile and oxidises readily, and the leaf's phenolics brown through polyphenol oxidase when bruised, which is why pesto is made quickly, cold, with oil as an oxygen barrier, and why basil blackens when cooked or refrigerated. Its affinity for tomato is a real aroma-chemistry match — tomato's green C6 aldehydes and its own linalool/methyl salicylate notes overlap with basil's. The fat in olive oil and cheese is also the solvent that carries the linalool to the nose, so basil tastes stronger in a fatty dish.
culinary.solubility: fat-soluble volatiles; rosmarinic acid water-soluble
culinary.when_to_add: raw or at the very end; tear rather than chop to limit enzymatic browning; Thai basil can take brief wok heat
culinary.heat_stability: poor — linalool is lost quickly; the anisic estragole-type survives heat better, which is partly why Thai cooking stir-fries basil and Italian cooking does not
culinary.antimicrobial_preservative: linalool, eugenol and estragole all have in vitro antimicrobial activity; basil oil is studied as a food preservative
culinary.digestive_tradition: carminative and anti-nausea in Mediterranean and Ayurvedic practice

claims.claim: linalool-type basil oil is calming / anxiolytic

aromatherapy.notes: Tisserand & Young distinguish the chemotypes sharply: linalool-type basil oil has a relatively generous dermal maximum, while estragole-rich ('exotic') basil oil is restricted to a low dermal maximum and methyleugenol-rich basil oil lower still, with pregnancy and child contraindications.

evidence_based.use: no approved clinical indication; no EMA monograph for Ocimum basilicum located

cautions.toxicity: The culinary herb is food. The regulatory and toxicological concern is estragole, which EFSA regards as genotoxic and carcinogenic in rodents; EFSA has issued opinions on estragole and on basil-containing preparations, and declined to set a safe intake for estragole. The estragole- and methyleugenol-rich oils are the hazardous forms, not the salad leaf.
cautions.pregnancy: Culinary use customary; the concentrated oils (especially estragole/methyleugenol chemotypes) should be avoided.

drug_interactions.mechanism: vitamin K1 in the fresh leaf (relevant only in large, variable intakes)
mild hypotensive effect of extracts in animals

cautions.allergen: occasional contact dermatitis to the oil; Lamiaceae oral allergy uncommon

strengthens.what: antimicrobial activity of other phenolic herbs in food systems
strengthens.why: additive membrane disruption by linalool plus eugenol/thymol-class phenols

herb_herb.effect: overlapping but distinct — holy basil is eugenol-led

EU: EFSA has published opinions on estragole and on the use of basil preparations; methyleugenol is likewise restricted.

in vitro microsomal inhibition; some human PK signals at supplement doses

plants.smell: earthy, slightly musty-woody and faintly ginger-camphoraceous; much less aromatic than it is coloured
plants.taste: earthy, bitter, slightly astringent and pungent; thin on its own, which is why it is almost never used alone

culinary.why: Turmeric's culinary job is two-thirds colour and one-third earthy bitterness; its aroma contribution is modest, which is why it functions as a base note under more aromatic spices rather than as a lead. Curcumin is a diketone with keto-enol tautomerism and it is strongly pH-sensitive: yellow in acid and neutral conditions, shifting to red-brown above about pH 8-9 — the reason turmeric-coloured food turns reddish in alkaline batters and the basis of the classic turmeric-paper alkali test. Curcumin is fat-soluble and very poorly water-soluble, so it must be bloomed in hot oil to distribute and to deepen in colour, and it is markedly light-sensitive, which is why turmeric-dyed fabric and turmeric-coloured food fade in sunlight. Its traditional pairing with black pepper and with fat is, unusually for folklore, mechanistically correct: piperine blocks curcumin's glucuronidation and efflux, and fat aids its absorption.
flavour_compounds: curcumin (colour and bitterness rather than aroma)
culinary.solubility: curcumin is fat- and alcohol-soluble, essentially water-insoluble; the turmerones are fat-soluble volatiles
culinary.when_to_add: bloom in hot fat early — both to develop colour and because raw turmeric tastes chalky; add at the start of a curry base
culinary.heat_stability: curcumin is reasonably heat-stable but degrades with prolonged heat, alkaline pH and especially light
culinary.antimicrobial_preservative: curcumin and the oil have in vitro antimicrobial and antifungal activity; turmeric's traditional use on wounds and in preserving has that basis
culinary.digestive_tradition: a core Ayurvedic digestive, anti-inflammatory and 'blood purifier'; applied topically on wounds and as a cosmetic

dye.colour: brilliant yellow to golden orange; shifts red-brown in alkali
dye.mordant: a direct (substantive) dye on protein fibres and needs no mordant, which is why it is the classic 'beginner' natural dye; alum improves it slightly on cellulose
dye.fibre: wool, silk and cotton; traditional for monastic saffron-coloured robes in South and Southeast Asia
dye.notes: Notoriously FUGITIVE — curcumin is highly photolabile and turmeric-dyed cloth fades rapidly in sunlight, which is why Cardon and other authorities class it as a fun but non-permanent dye. It is also the dye on classic 'turmeric paper' alkali indicator, and the food colour E100.
dye.source: Cardon D., Natural Dyes: Sources, Tradition, Technology and Science (recalled, not re-pulled); natural-dye practice

claims.claim: turmeric oil is anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial

aromatherapy.notes: Turmeric oil is a turmerone oil carrying no curcumin, so aromatherapy turmeric does not deliver the pharmacology turmeric is famous for. Mildly irritant; Tisserand & Young give a moderate dermal maximum.

traditional: haridra in Ayurveda — anti-inflammatory, wound healing, skin, digestion, 'blood purifier'
jiang huang in TCM for blood stasis and pain
topical paste for wounds, acne and ceremonial use

evidence_based.source: meta-analyses of curcumin extracts show a modest benefit, though trials are small, heterogeneous and often industry-linked

evidence_based.use: the very broad anticancer, Alzheimer's, depression and metabolic claims
evidence_based.source: enormous preclinical literature that has repeatedly failed to translate, largely because of the bioavailability problem; curcumin is a textbook example of an in vitro 'hit' that does not reach tissue after oral dosing

evidence_based.use: EMA: Curcumae longae rhizoma monograph covers traditional use in mild digestive complaints
evidence_based.source: monograph existence recalled; not re-verified this session

cautions.toxicity: Culinary use is safe and long-established. Supplement-dose curcumin is a different matter: hepatotoxicity has been reported in a growing number of cases, especially with 'enhanced-bioavailability' formulations (piperine-containing or phytosome products), and LiverTox-type registries now list turmeric/curcumin as a recognised cause of drug-induced liver injury. High oxalate content makes high-dose turmeric a kidney-stone risk in susceptible people. Lead chromate adulteration of turmeric is a documented and serious public-health problem in some supply chains.
cautions.pregnancy: Culinary use customary. Supplement doses are not recommended — traditional emmenagogue reputation plus uterine-stimulant activity in animals.

drug_interactions.mechanism: curcumin inhibits platelet aggregation in vitro and case reports describe raised INR with turmeric supplements

drug_interactions.drug_or_class: CYP3A4 substrates (including tacrolimus, where a case of toxicity is documented)
drug_interactions.mechanism: CYP3A4 and P-gp inhibition at supplement doses
curcumin saturates and competes for UGT capacity
additive glucose lowering reported in trials
curcumin chelates iron and has caused iron deficiency in a case report at high intake
deliberately raises curcumin exposure — which also raises the hepatotoxicity and interaction risk; the potentiation is real and cuts both ways

cautions.photosensitivity: curcumin is a photosensitiser in vitro (it is used as a photodynamic agent in research), but clinical phototoxicity from dietary turmeric is not established
cautions.allergen: contact dermatitis to curcumin reported; uncommon

strengthens.what: co-administered drugs cleared by CYP3A4, P-gp or glucuronidation
strengthens.why: curcumin inhibits all three at supplement concentrations

herb_herb.effect: the canonical potentiation pair — piperine dramatically raises curcumin bioavailability
herb_herb.why: piperine blocks intestinal glucuronidation and P-gp efflux of curcumin

herb_herb.effect: additive anti-inflammatory in vitro; the common supplement pairing

herb_herb.with: fat (not an herb, but the key practical co-factor)
herb_herb.why: curcumin is lipophilic and absorption improves with lipids

regulatory: US: turmeric and turmeric oleoresin are GRAS (21 CFR 182.10, 182.20) and turmeric/turmeric oleoresin are approved colour additives exempt from certification (21 CFR 73.600, 73.615).
EU: curcumin is the authorised food colour E100.
EU: EMA HMPC monograph for Curcumae longae rhizoma (traditional use).

Safety alerts: multiple jurisdictions have issued recalls for lead-chromate-adulterated turmeric, and hepatotoxicity signals have prompted regulatory review of high-dose curcumin supplements in some countries.

plants.smell: sweet, creamy, balsamic-woody with a smoky-phenolic depth; Tahitian adds a floral-anisic, cherry-like note
plants.taste: sweet-aromatic, slightly bitter in the whole bean; perceived as sweetening without sugar

culinary.why: Vanilla is the key worked example of flavour as a product of enzymatic processing rather than of the raw plant: the green pod is odourless, and curing (killing, sweating, drying, conditioning over weeks to months) lets the bean's own beta-glucosidase cleave glucovanillin to free vanillin. Vanillin is fat- and alcohol-soluble and only sparingly water-soluble, which is why it is infused into cream, butter or alcohol rather than water, and why extract is made in ethanol. It also enhances perceived sweetness and creaminess — a well-documented cross-modal effect — so a custard with vanilla needs less sugar. Its aroma is congruent with the Maillard and caramel compounds of baked goods, which is why it blends into almost any sweet system without reading as a separate flavour.
culinary.solubility: alcohol- and fat-soluble; poorly water-soluble
culinary.when_to_add: infuse the split pod into warm (not boiling) cream or milk and steep off the heat; add extract at the end of cooking because ethanol and the volatiles flash off
culinary.heat_stability: vanillin is reasonably heat-stable but the delicate top notes are lost on hard boiling; alcohol extract loses aroma with the alcohol
culinary.antimicrobial_preservative: vanillin has genuine in vitro antimicrobial and antifungal activity and is studied as a food preservative
culinary.digestive_tradition: minor; historically a carminative and 'nervine' in European pharmacy

claims.claim: calming and comforting; vanilla odour reduced startle response and distress in some studies
vanilla 'essential oil' does not exist — the aromatherapy article is a CO2 extract, absolute or oleoresin

aromatherapy.notes: Vanilla absolute/extract is low-risk dermally; vanillin is a recognised but uncommon contact sensitiser, and 'vanilla' fragrance materials are a common cosmetic allergen source.

traditional: nervine and 'aphrodisiac' in 18th-19th century European pharmacy

evidence_based.use: odour-mediated calming / analgesic adjunct in neonates
evidence_based.source: small clinical studies of vanilla odour

cautions.toxicity: Food, very low risk. The real hazard is adulteration: 'Mexican vanilla' sold cheaply has repeatedly been found to be tonka-bean-based or coumarin-added, and coumarin is prohibited as a food additive in the US (21 CFR 189.130) and hepatotoxic in quantity.
cautions.pregnancy: No concern at food use.

drug_interactions.mechanism: only relevant if the product is coumarin-adulterated — and note plain coumarin is not itself a vitamin-K antagonist; the concern is hepatic

cautions.allergen: vanillin contact allergy exists (and cross-reacts with balsam of Peru); 'vanilla' fragrance sensitisation is reported

strengthens.what: perceived sweetness and creaminess of a food
strengthens.why: cross-modal odour-taste integration, well documented in sensory science

regulatory: US: vanilla and vanilla extract have a standard of identity (21 CFR 169) specifying extraction strength; 'vanilla flavoring' and 'imitation' labelling are regulated.
US: coumarin prohibited as a food additive (21 CFR 189.130) — the legal basis for action against tonka-adulterated 'vanilla'.
EU: vanillin is a permitted flavouring substance; vanilla is a food.
